content.thinking:
I'm putting the postmortem together from the key facts: a HighLatency alert on io-shop with no deploys or flag changes, onset at 03:15. The capacity flip between 3 and 6 cores from 03:11 is confirmed, and raising the autoscaler floor from 3 to 6 as mitigation is confirmed too. The Code-Fix F1 points at scaleDownStabilizationSeconds set to 0 as the cause of flapping, but no S or D row backs that up yet.

I'm weighing whether the flip-flopping capacity is actually established as the cause, since the stabilization-window reading comes only from the fix candidate, so I'll treat it as stated. For the trigger, I can't point to a confirmed change, so I'll cite the timeline rows and the mitigation evidence instead of the candidate labels.

I'm working out the causal chain for the postmortem: shop requests slowed while the service ran at its lower replica count, and raising the floor to 6 put it back. The autoscaler kept scaling it down to 3, which is where the flip-flopping comes from, and I'm citing the timeline rows and mitigation evidence for each step.

I'm checking the ruled-out items for step three: no deploys in the day before 03:16, and no flag changes in the hour before 03:23, so neither can account for the onset. That leaves the autoscaler's own behaviour as the trigger, and step four names the stabilization window set to zero as the root cause.

I'm settling on the root cause as the scale-down stabilization window being set to zero, which lets the autoscaler pull replicas back as soon as its own scale-up lowers per-replica CPU. Since that setting comes only from the fix candidate, I'll note the cause rests on that unrun reading.

I'm checking whether the floor and the max still leave room to flap: with the floor at 6 and the max also at 6, the autoscaler can't swing between 3 and 6 anymore, though demand above what six replicas can serve would still go unmet.

Checking whether the floor-equals-max setup still leaves room for growth: with the floor and the ceiling both at 6, the autoscaler can't flap between 3 and 6 anymore, but it also can't add capacity past six replicas if demand keeps rising.

I'm noting that nobody was paged, since no on-call incident was linked to the alert on the production shop, though a page would not have shortened the incident. Next I'm moving on to the autoscaler as a possible check to make.

I'm writing up the contributing factors now, starting with the missing configuration check that would have caught the zero scale-down window before it reached production. I'm proposing a CI rule that rejects that value for production.

I'm drafting the contributing factors and action items for the postmortem. For the detection gap, I'm noting that no alert on the autoscaler repeatedly scaling up and down was seen, so the fault surfaced only through the latency alert. I'm proposing an alert on the replica count changing direction repeatedly. The prevention and process items are next, starting with a CI check for the zero stabilization window and linking the HighLatency alert to on-call paging.

I'm pulling together the lessons: the investigator ruled out deploys and flag changes, Argus checked the flag history, and the mitigation agent raised the floor on time. Code-Fix's draft PR is the other thing worth naming. The only gap I can point to is that nobody was paged.

I'm settling the assumptions: the mechanism leans on Code-Fix's reading of the production values file, since the record never shows the running autoscaler's setting was read. And the rising demand that made the autoscaler scale up at all comes from the investigation's account, not from any row in the timeline.

I'm lining up the postmortem's evidence for each step of the causal chain: the step about slowed responses rests on the rows showing too little serving capacity, while the step about the autoscaler pulling replicas back down to its floor depends on the timeline row and the fix candidate's reading. I'm also noting that deploys and flag changes are ruled out as the trigger.

I'm settling the symptom wording: shop responses slowed sharply, which I'll state without a number, and I'm now working on how to describe the impact of the slow requests in plain terms.

I'm settling the wording for the impact: the slowest requests took far longer than usual, while failures stayed within normal variation.

action_items.item: Add a CI check that rejects production autoscaler values with a scale-down stabilization window of zero, or below an agreed minimum, for every service.
Add an alert that fires when a service's autoscaler keeps reversing its replica count within a short window.
Link io-shop's HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: People using the shop got much slower responses: its slowest requests took far longer than usual, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation.
Responses slowed because io-shop had too little serving capacity for the requests coming in.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop: none were found in the day before the onset
A feature flag change: the flag provider showed no changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before it was read

causal_chain.step: It had too little capacity because the autoscaler did not hold the higher replica count. It kept taking the service back down to its floor of {T7.2} replicas, the count read at {T7.1}.

The autoscaler scaled back down straight away because the production values set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds. That let it act on the low per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, because a setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set to zero, and that left too few servers to answer requests quickly.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that would have stopped a production autoscaler configuration with a scale-down stabilization window of zero from going out.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The window would have stayed at a non-zero value such as the default. The autoscaler would then have held its scale-up, and capacity would not have kept dropping back to the floor.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No alert was seen on the autoscaler repeatedly scaling io-shop up and back down. The fault was found only by the latency alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The flapping could have been caught from the replica count itself, before slow responses had gone on long enough to set off the latency alert.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: Argus read the flag provider's history and ruled out flag changes before acting.
The Mitigation Agent raised io-shop's autoscaler floor, an action that can be put back.
The Investigator Agent checked production changes and found no deploys or releases, so the search for a cause did not chase a change that never happened.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix to the autoscaler configuration as draft pull request #544 for a person to review.

went_wrong: The alert fired on the production shop, but no on-call incident was linked to it, so nobody was paged.

input.root_cause: The production values for io-shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds. As Code-Fix reads it, after scaling up from {F1.1} to {F1.2} replicas, the controller acted straight away on the lower per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced. It scaled back to {F1.1} replicas, where CPU was pinned again, so serving capacity kept flipping up and down instead of holding.
input.still_at_risk: While the scale-down window in the shop's configuration stays at zero, the autoscaler could again drop the shop back to too few replicas as soon as its floor is lowered, and responses could slow again.
input.symptom: Shop requests responded far more slowly than usual
